title: Flying to the United States
subtitle: Booking a flight, reconfirming it, and getting through passport control — with the words you actually need.
description: An A2 listening and reading page with three model dialogues: booking a flight by phone, reconfirming a reservation, and answering questions at US passport control.
passage: Three short conversations you are likely to have on the way to the United States. The traveler's lines are filled in here as models — read them, then cover them and try your own.
1. BOOKING A FLIGHT BY PHONE
Clerk: Northwind Airlines, good morning. May I help you?
You: Good morning. Do you have any flights to Chicago next Tuesday afternoon?
Clerk: One moment, please… Yes. There's a flight at 4:45 p.m. and one at 6:00 p.m.
You: How much is the 4:45, and how long does it take?
Clerk: Economy, business or first class?
You: Economy, please.
Clerk: That would be three hundred and forty-six dollars, round trip.
You: All right. I'd like to book the 4:45 flight, please.
Clerk: Certainly. Could I have your name, please?
You: It's Karen Jones. That's J-O-N-E-S.
Clerk: And how would you like to pay, Ms. Jones?
You: By credit card. Can I give you the number now?
Clerk: Yes, but please note you'll need to check in at least two hours before departure.
You: Two hours. Got it, thank you.
Clerk: You're booked, Ms. Jones. The flight leaves at 4:45 p.m. and arrives in Chicago at 9:25 p.m. local time. The flight number is NWA 476.
You: Could you repeat the flight number, please?
2. RECONFIRMING A RESERVATION
Clerk: Northwind Airlines. Can I help you?
You: Yes — I'd like to reconfirm my flight, please.
Clerk: May I have your name and flight number?
You: David Adams, flight NWA 118.
Clerk: When are you leaving?
You: On the fourteenth, next Friday.
Clerk: And your destination?
You: Miami.
Clerk: Hold the line, please… All right, your seat is confirmed, Mr. Adams. You'll arrive in Miami at 4:00 p.m. local time.
You: Thank you. Is there anything else I need to do?
Clerk: Just check in at least an hour before departure.
3. AT PASSPORT CONTROL
Officer: Good evening. Where have you come from?
You: From São Paulo, on flight NWA 476.
Officer: May I see your passport, please?
You: Here you are.
Officer: What's the purpose of your visit — business or pleasure?
You: Business. I'm attending a conference in Chicago.
Officer: How long are you going to stay in the United States?
You: Ten days. I'm flying home on the twenty-fourth.
Officer: What do you do for a living?
You: I'm a software engineer.
Officer: Do you have a return ticket?
You: Yes, I do. Would you like to see it?
Officer: That's fine. Thank you — enjoy your trip.
You: Thank you very much.

vocabulary.definition: there and back (American English; British: return)
to arrange a seat or room in advance
to check again that your booking is still valid
to register at the airport before a flight, or at a hotel on arrival
the official phrase for why you are traveling
the standard choice officers offer: for work, or for a vacation
what you say as you hand something to someone

vocabulary.term: What do you do for a living?
vocabulary.definition: a natural way to ask someone's occupation

exercises.title: What Would You Say?
exercises.instructions: Choose the best response in each situation.

items.explanation: The question offers a choice, so name the one you want.

items.prompt: Clerk: "Could I have your name, please?"
items.explanation: Give the name. "Yes, you could" answers the words but not the request.

items.prompt: Officer: "What's the purpose of your visit?"
items.explanation: The purpose is why you came. 'Ten days' answers how long, and 'From São Paulo' answers where from.

items.prompt: Officer: "How long are you going to stay?"
Officer: "Do you have a return ticket?"
options: Yes, I do. Would you like to see it?
items.explanation: Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Do you…? — Yes, I do.

items.prompt: You did not hear the flight number. You say:
items.explanation: "Could you repeat that, please?" is the polite standard.

items.prompt: I'd like a ___ trip ticket to Chicago, please.
items.explanation: American English says 'round trip'; British English says 'return'.

items.prompt: Please ___ in at least two hours before departure.
items.explanation: You check in at the airport before a flight.

items.prompt: I called the airline to ___ my flight.
items.explanation: To reconfirm is to check again that your booking is valid.
Departure is leaving; arrival is getting there.
"Hold the line" is the fixed telephone phrase for 'please wait'.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the dialogues.

items.statement: Ms. Jones books the 6:00 p.m. flight.
items.explanation: False — she books the 4:45 p.m. flight.

items.statement: She must check in two hours before departure.
items.explanation: True — the clerk says at least two hours.

items.statement: Mr. Adams is flying to Chicago.
The traveler at passport control came for a vacation.
items.explanation: False — the purpose is business: a conference in Chicago.

items.statement: The officer asks to see the return ticket.
items.explanation: False — the traveler offers it, but the officer says "That's fine" without looking.

discussion: Role-play dialogue 1 with a partner: one of you is the clerk, the other books a flight to a city of your choice.
Have you ever been asked questions at passport control? What did they ask, and how did you answer?
Officers ask short, direct questions. Why do you think short, complete answers work better than long explanations?
Write a telephone dialogue (about 10 lines) in which you change a booking you already made.
